The section also notes that stacking CONV layers increases feature complexity deeper in the network.

The section frames the supervised learning problem used in the chapter — predicting magnetic field distributions from geometric, excitation, and material features — and outlines the ML pipeline (data collection, network architectures, network operation, tuning, and results) pointing to subsequent sections. It also highlights the need to detect out-of-distribution inputs and to perform uncertainty analysis so the DL emulator can better replicate physics-based judgment.

This LaTeX section documents the Data Collection process used to build training datasets for DL-based magnetic field estimation. It explains dataset concepts (task/domain, supervised learning, classification vs. regression) and emphasizes the importance of representative input data. The implementation strategy is to represent inputs as CAD geometry augmented with material and excitation information sampled at sufficient resolution and organized on a uniform structured grid (one input 'pixel' per grid node). Sample generation is done via parametric CAD models and FEA simulations in the MAGNET package (using material properties including nonlinear B–H curves). Samples are populated using Latin Hypercube sampling to cover parameter space. Three progressively complex, parameterized electromagnetic problems are generated as datasets: a single copper coil in an air box (coil radius, center position and current varied), a two-coil transformer with an M19 silicon-steel core (geometric ranges tabulated; left coil excited), and a 4-pole, 24-slot interior permanent magnet (IPM) motor (multiple geometric magnet/stator parameters and winding currents varied; partial one-pole model used). The section also notes the need to handle out-of-distribution inputs and describes using uncertainty analysis to mitigate physics-inconsistent predictions. The following section introduces Neural Networks.

This LaTeX section documents the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) used in the thesis: it explains CNN fundamentals (convolutional, pooling and fully‑connected layers), motivates convolutional assumptions for structured spatial data, and describes the specific encoder–decoder CNN architecture implemented and trained. The model was trained by backpropagation to minimize RMS error between predictions and FEA field distributions on a dataset sampled by Latin Hypercube (30,000 train / 10,000 val / 5,000 test). The section also covers model selection (35 candidate networks, grid/random search), the observed benefit of dilated filters for this regression/segmentation‑style task, and the rationale for architectural choices (bottleneck/latent representation, locality vs. context trade‑off).

entities.entity_name: Chp2_CNN::Architecture of the CNN based model
entities.description: This LaTeX subsection documents the CNN-based model architecture used in the work. It explains the three basic layer types (convolution, pooling, fully‑connected) and describes the specific implemented encoder–decoder CNN: a 32‑layer network with 16 trainable convolutional layers, eight pooling/up‑sampling layers and eight dropout layers (~2.4M parameters). Each encoder/decoder block contains two 3×3 convolutional layers (ReLU + batch‑normalization) followed by 2×2 max‑pooling or up‑sampling with stride 2 (convolutions use stride 1); the last two convolutional layers deviate from this pattern to match the field‑distribution dimensionality. The subsection also notes the use of dilated filters to capture long‑range spatial relationships, training by backpropagation to minimize RMS error against FEA field outputs, input sampling via a Latin Hypercube over geometry/excitation limits, and dataset splits (30,000 train / 10,000 validation / 5,000 test). In short, it provides a concise specification of the network topology, layer details, training objective and dataset preparation for the CNN surrogate model.

This LaTeX subsection documents how the convolutional deep learning model works for dense regression of field solutions. It explains the encoder–decoder architecture (encoder compresses to a latent representation, decoder projects features back to the input space), the need to balance model capacity and regularization, and the hyperparameter search process (35 candidate networks, using grid/random search). The text highlights that increasing layers and filter counts helps but that the largest performance gain came from adding dilated convolutional filters and skip connections (example best configuration: kernel size 5, K=64, alternate dilated layers in the encoder). It reports that dilation improves normalized RMS prediction error across three problems (with similar accuracy for K=32 and K=64 in one case) and gives the physical intuition that dilation increases the receptive field so distant source effects can be captured without larger kernels. A training-curve figure illustrating validation prediction error is referenced.

This LaTeX section (Results & Performance) in Chp2_CNN reports the empirical performance of the CNN-based field predictor. The text notes that non-linear materials were included but the network degrades if excitations differ significantly from the training set. Computational details are provided: training on an NVIDIA 1080 Ti at ≈10 minutes per epoch with batch size 16, convergence in ~60–100 epochs (≈12–15 hours total), and inference of 100 geometries in ~2–3 seconds (memory-limited when scaling). The section includes figures illustrating the problem, network architecture, predictions, FEA results, and the error distribution, and it precedes a following section on Uncertainty Prediction.

A LaTeX section in Chp2_CNN titled "Uncertainty Prediction" that describes how to obtain and use prediction uncertainty for a convolutional neural network via Monte Carlo (MC) dropout. It motivates the need for uncertainty maps for supervised DL models (especially on out-of-distribution inputs), explains the theoretical basis (casting dropout as approximate Bayesian/variational inference and approximating the intractable weight posterior with Monte Carlo integration), and gives the practical recipe: train with dropout and perform multiple stochastic forward passes at test time to sample the approximate posterior over weights and produce per-pixel uncertainty maps. The section relates this approach to Bayesian SegNet, discusses interpreting softmax outputs vs. uncertainty, and suggests using uncertainty thresholds for more reliable segmentation. This LaTeX subsection documents the concept of "Uncertainty Maps" for CNN-based pixel classification. It explains that softmax outputs should not be naively treated as confidence scores (noting vulnerability to adversarial perturbations), and describes using dropout at inference (Monte Carlo dropout, per Gal et al.) to treat network weights as distributions and extract predictive uncertainty. The text motivates generating per-pixel uncertainty maps to locate regions where the model is unsure and suggests using an uncertainty threshold to produce a partial but highly reliable segmentation. (This is explanatory documentation rather than executable code; the following subsection provides the theoretical details.)

This LaTeX subsection provides the theoretical background for using dropout as approximate Bayesian inference in convolutional neural networks. It explains that training with dropout can be seen as learning an approximate posterior over weights (q(W)) via variational inference by minimizing KL divergence to the true posterior, that the true posterior and evidence are intractable, and that performing dropout at test time yields Monte Carlo samples (MC dropout) from the approximate posterior by drawing Bernoulli-distributed weight masks and averaging stochastic forward passes. The text connects this theory to prior work (e.g., Bayesian SegNet), motivates producing uncertainty maps for segmentation, and frames uncertainty estimation as an outcome of sampling the dropout-induced weight distribution rather than adding extra parameters.

This LaTeX section presents the Bayesian Network results for the CNNs: it explains how Monte Carlo (MC) dropout is used to produce uncertainty maps by taking 10 stochastic forward passes through each network, computing the standard deviation across the softmax outputs of those samples (then averaging the per-class standard deviations to produce a single uncertainty map). It references a figure with (a) error distribution, (b) normalized uncertainty map, and (c) zoomed regions of high uncertainty, and reports that MC sampling both correlates with regions of high prediction error (identifying two of three high-error regions) and improved classification accuracy (normalized MSE) by about 10%. The writeup also notes that high uncertainty should discourage reliance on the network’s output and may prompt use of conventional solvers (FEA, FDM, etc.).

This LaTeX section documents the data-collection pipeline used to generate training data for predicting motor efficiency maps. It specifies a four-stage procedure: (1) run electromagnetic FE simulations at several dq current points to obtain dq flux linkages and fit 2nd-degree polynomial flux-linkage maps (λd, λq), (2) compute optimal excitation conditions (Is*, γ*) per speed using control strategies (MTPA, Flux Weakening, MTPV), (3) run FE simulations at those operating points to obtain electromagnetic torque and efficiency (Tem*, η*), and (4) post-process and interpolate the (N*, Tem*, η*) samples to produce an efficiency map. The section also describes the dataset generation for a parametrized 24-slot 4-pole IPM motor: Latin Hypercube sampling of 2,900 designs with ±50% variation on reference parameters, partitioning into 2,500 train / 200 validation / 200 test samples, and roughly 120 FE simulations per motor for the Stage-1 and Stage-3 computations. Figures (flowchart and motor geometry) and a table of design parameters are referenced. Metadata locates this section in Chp3_RNN (label RNN:3_dataCollection).

This section defines the neural-network based surrogate models used to replace costly finite-element (FE) simulations in the workflow. It specifies two primary architectures and a modular strategy: (1) A hybrid ANN–CNN surrogate for Stage 1 (Flux Linkage Calculation) that takes parametrized CAD geometry/material-distribution as a pixel image into a CNN and current excitation (Is, γ) as a 1‑D vector into a feedforward ANN; the CNN output is flattened and merged with the ANN hidden vector and passed through a second feedforward network to predict dq flux linkages. (2) A sequence-based surrogate for Stage 3 (Torque and Efficiency Calculation) that uses an RNN encoder (with shared RNN cell weights to support variable sequence lengths) augmented with an attention mechanism to capture long-range and local dependencies across torque-speed points; a time-distributed dense (feedforward) decoder combines the attention-weighted encoder outputs with global context (geometry) to produce a sequence of efficiency values. The section also describes an alternative end-to-end approach: a symmetric CNN encoder–decoder that predicts normalized 2D efficiency maps directly from structured geometry/material inputs, plus a supplementary network that predicts per-design peak torque/speed to denormalize the map. Overall, the entity documents inputs, outputs, model fusion, handling of variable-length sequences, and the motivation for using attention and time-distributed decoding to improve prediction accuracy and generalization across many design variants.

This subsection documents the modular neural-network pipeline used to predict motor dq flux linkages and, from those, per-design efficiency maps. The implementation is split into stages and sub-networks: (1) A three-part flux-linkage model where a CNN ingests pixelated CAD geometry/material distribution and a feedforward ANN encodes current excitation (I_s, γ); their hidden outputs are flattened/concatenated and passed to a second feedforward network which predicts dq flux linkages for each design sample. (2) Predicted dq flux linkages are interpolated to produce flux maps and used to compute optimal control points (N*, I_s*, γ*) for each torque–speed operating point. (3) A sequence-based surrogate (Stage 3) predicts efficiency sequences for those operating points: for each time step the model receives five inputs (N*, I_s*, γ*, T_em*, N_base*). The encoder is an RNN whose initial/context state is seeded with geometric information (either parameter vectors or the CNN encoding); an attention mechanism is applied over encoder outputs to reduce information loss for long sequences (≈120–170 steps). A time-distributed dense (feedforward) decoder consumes the attention-weighted encoder outputs plus the global context and produces the sequence of efficiency values. The design handles variable-length sequences via RNN weight sharing and time-distributed layers.

This subsection describes an alternative end-to-end deep‑learning approach for predicting motor efficiency maps directly from CAD geometry and material distribution. The input is a 2D structured representation that encodes geometry/material information; the target is a uniform 2D grid of efficiency values where each sample’s speed (N*) and electromagnetic torque (T_em*) are normalized to 1. A symmetric encoder–decoder CNN (shown in the referenced figure) produces the normalized efficiency map, thereby avoiding intermediate steps such as flux‑linkage map generation and excitation/control calculations. Because the predicted map is normalized, a separate CNN‑style network is trained to predict the absolute peak speed and torque from the CAD plus additional 3D geometric metadata (e.g., stack length). The outputs of both networks are combined to reconstruct the absolute efficiency map for a design.

This LaTeX section documents the experimental results and discussion for supervised deep-learning models in Chapter 3. This section defines the transfer-learning methodology used to accelerate and improve deep‑neural‑network (DNN) prediction of motor performance maps. It describes dataset generation (motor geometry parameters varied ±50% around a reference, Latin‑Hypercube sampling to produce 3200 designs, split into 2500/200/200 training/validation/test with 300 held out), and the pipeline for computing performance maps via electromagnetic finite‑element (FE) simulations (torque, efficiency, power factor) with two DNNs used as surrogates for FE Stages 1 and 3. The implemented TL procedure uses greedy layer‑wise pretraining: identify and freeze pre‑trained layers that capture prior knowledge, replace remaining layers with new randomly‑initialized layers, train the new layers, then fine‑tune the whole network (with a reduced learning rate, typically an order of magnitude lower) to adapt to the target task. Describes how the motor-design data and corresponding performance maps are generated for the transfer-learning study. Two deep neural networks are used as surrogate models to replace FE computations in stages of this pipeline. This subsection specifies the transfer-learning procedure used in the RNN chapter. Conclusion section summarizing the chapter’s findings: learning an efficiency-map representation enables various neural-network models to act as accurate surrogates for FE simulations on geometries similar to training data. entities.description: This LaTeX subsubsection ("3. Why use ON/OFF based TO") explains the rationale, advantages and drawbacks of ON/OFF (binary) topology-optimization methods. It summarizes benefits—primarily implementation convenience and easy integration with FEA tools—and contrasts them with heuristic/global-search approaches that can be computationally expensive. It gives a concrete example of the high computational cost when using a genetic algorithm for a PM motor, and discusses common solution artifacts (floating material, checkerboarding, staircase patterns) and mitigation strategies (filtering/smoothing and adding smoothness objectives). It also highlights limitations of heuristics versus deterministic/density-based methods (heavy computation, lack of guaranteed connectivity, and tuning/filter-parameter issues). The subsection serves to motivate and contextualize subsequent material on improving ON/OFF TO methodology.

This subsection introduces a novel improvement to ON/OFF topology optimization (TO): a sequence-based TO method that enforces connectivity among same-material cells to eliminate checkerboards, perforations and floating material, yielding more manufacturable designs without applying filtering, smoothing, or objective modification. The method is designed to be compatible with heuristic tree-search approaches (e.g., Reinforcement Learning/Q‑learning) and is validated on problems such as a C‑core actuator and a synchronous reluctance motor rotor. The subsection also notes that this methodology will be extended in the next chapter to enable generalization to previously unseen design problems, reducing the computational cost of evolutionary discrete TO. (Entity: LaTeX subsection; metadata: Subsection, definition)

A sequence-based topology-optimization controller that acts as a movable block of cells on a discretized design grid. The controller is defined by its size (an s×s footprint) and an associated material; it moves one step at a time according to selected actions (e.g. left/right/up/down) and leaves a trail of material in the cells it occupies. The optimization task is cast as searching for a sequence of controller actions that yields an optimal material distribution. Movement is constrained by domain boundaries (excitation source, air, symmetry), and for multi-cell controllers the current position is referenced by a central pointer. This description corresponds to the SeqTO-v1 formulation.

The controller can have varying physical size, which determines how much material it can deposit per action. The controller’s location is marked by a pointer that distinguishes it from the deposited trail; for multi-element controllers the pointer is the centermost grid point. This LaTeX section (Topology Optimization with SeqTO-v1) documents the optimization methodology used in Chapter 4. It (1) motivates and summarizes the use of a Genetic Algorithm (GA) — implemented with MATLAB’s Global Optimization toolbox and based on prior work — for discrete ON/OFF and sequence-based (SeqTO-v1) topology optimization, including GA operators, termination considerations, and parameter choices tied to the controller and sequence length; (2) defines a sequence-based optimization problem for a C‑core electromagnetic actuator: the decision variable is an action sequence a (each action in {0,1,2,3}) of length m that populates a binary material vector p over a 2D half‑symmetric design grid of 288 cells, the objective f(a) is the negative armature force (minimization), and a volume constraint enforces K1≤#(p_j=1)≤K2 (K1=80, K2=180); (3) describes the C‑core geometry, discretization (1 mm cells, 40 mm depth), controller behavior (starting position, allowed steps), and how controller steps map to material placement; and (4) introduces tree‑search / sequence decision algorithms (TD learning, Monte Carlo / RL) as alternative approaches, with a brief comparison between reinforcement learning and evolutionary algorithms. The entity provides the problem formulation, modeling details, and rationale for choosing GA and potential RL extensions.

This subsection describes a Genetic Algorithm (GA) optimization setup used to design a C-core electromagnetic actuator. The GA searches for an action sequence a (length m, each action taking one of a small discrete set) that a controller executes to populate a binary material-distribution vector p over a half‑symmetric 2D design grid (n = 288 cells, depth fixed at 40 mm). The objective f(a) is the negative of the magnetic pull on the armature (so the GA minimizes f to maximize force). A volume constraint enforces that the number of steel cells switched on (p_j = 1) lies between K1 = 80 and K2 = 180. The controller starts at a fixed location, and m is chosen so the controller can place slightly more than K2 cells to allow for wasted moves. The implementation uses MATLAB’s Global Optimization GA toolbox (informed by Midha 2018); GA design variables are the m actions, population size is chosen as a multiple of m, and standard GA operators (selection, crossover, mutation, elitism) and termination criteria (generation count, time, or stall limits) are employed.

This LaTeX subsubsection defines the C-core electromagnetic actuator design and its formulation as a discrete material-distribution optimization problem driven by a sequence-based controller. It describes the physical model (a C-shaped electromagnet with coil, soft magnetic core (M-19) and armature), the design objective (maximize armature pull, expressed as minimization of the negative force f(a)), and the mapping from a controller action sequence a (each action a_i ∈ {0,1,2,3}) to a binary material vector p (cells: air p_j=0 or electrical steel p_j=1). The 2-D design domain is depth 40 mm, discretized into 288 symmetric 1 mm square cells (half-model used), with conventional C-core occupying 180 steel cells. Constraints enforce a volume limit K2=180 and exploration lower bound K1=80 on the number of steel cells. The sequence length m is a user-chosen hyperparameter equal to the controller’s maximum steps and is used as the number of GA design variables; GA population size is chosen as a multiple of m. The subsection also notes initialization (all-air), fixed controller start location, and the intent to apply GA variants (ON/OFF and SeqTO-v1) to optimize the controller sequence that produces the final material distribution.

This LaTeX subsection titled "Tree Search Algorithms" (label: section:MDP_TD_learning) introduces the use of sequence-based, tree-search-style methods for topology optimization (e.g., Temporal Difference learning, Monte Carlo methods, and related Dynamic Programming approaches). The entity includes a comparison table contrasting Reinforcement Learning and Evolutionary Algorithms, and concludes by stating that the work will focus on a TD-learning based algorithm (thus not covering broader RL algorithms).

This LaTeX section documents the Markov Decision Process (MDP) and temporal-difference (TD) learning concepts used in the thesis (Chapter 4, SeqTO-v1). It defines core MDP elements (environment, state, action, reward), policy types (deterministic vs stochastic), episodic task design and episode-length guidance for topology optimization, and reward-design considerations (including a C-core magnetic-field-based reward example). It explains state representation choices and the need to preserve the Markov property. The section introduces value functions (action-value Q(s,a) and state-value V(s)), motivates using Q(s,a) for this work, and contrasts Monte Carlo and TD approaches. It presents bootstrapping and the recursive return, TD-style incremental update formulas, the role of the discount factor γ in stabilizing learning, and the connection between TD, Monte Carlo, and dynamic programming via the Bellman optimality relation. The material sets up Q-learning as the next topic.

This LaTeX subsection defines the Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation used in the project (Chp4_MDP::Markov Decision Process). It converts the topology‑optimization task into a discrete-time sequential decision problem by specifying the core MDP elements: environment, state, action, reward, and controller–environment interaction. It describes the policy types used (deterministic policies for this work, with stochastic policies deferred), the episodic nature of the task and guidelines for choosing episode length (limited by material/volume constraints and number of FEM calls), and the return definition (cumulative reward). The text explains the reward design choices — notably using magnetic field distribution in the C‑core armature as a robust proxy for force — and shows situations producing negative rewards or design errors. It also discusses MDP dynamics and the Markov property (and how to include history in the state to preserve Markovian behavior), presents several state representation options (discrete design grid, B‑field augmented variants), and notes that the presented SeqTO‑v1 formulation is flexible and may be adapted in future work.

This LaTeX subsubsection defines the concept of a policy in a Markov Decision Process: a policy is a distribution over actions for each state. It contrasts deterministic policies—which map each state to a single action (π(s)=a) and can be represented in tabular form—with stochastic policies, which assign nonzero probabilities to multiple actions in a state. The text notes that action choices across states are independent, assumes the Markov property (the state contains all decision-relevant information), and states that the chapter focuses on deterministic policies while stochastic policies are deferred to a later chapter.

A LaTeX subsubsection that documents the choice of an episodic Markov Decision Process for the design optimization task. It explains why the task should be treated as episodic (limited material/volume and desire to limit function-evaluation calls), recommends limiting episode length to the minimum number of steps required to place the available material, and advises allowing roughly twice that number of steps per episode so the agent has sufficient opportunity to explore the design space. This LaTeX subsubsection defines the reward formulation used for the MDP in the C‑core topology optimization study. It explains design goals: the reward must encode both immediate and cumulative objectives under a material (volume) constraint so the agent balances short‑ and long‑term gains. Although the natural objective is the force on the armature, the text documents that force readings are noisy when the design domain contains little material, so the magnetic field distribution inside the armature is chosen as a more robust proxy (directly proportional to the magnetic flux through the armature). The section also states the standard return definition G_t = R_{t+1} + R_{t+2} + … + R_N and introduces the MDP dynamics heading.

This LaTeX subsubsection (MDP Dynamics) documents the Markov decision process formulation used in the thesis for sequential topology optimization (SeqTO-v1). It explains the required Markov property (future states and rewards depend only on the current state and action) and how to preserve it when agent behavior must depend on previous actions by augmenting the state with a trace of past design- and material-distribution information. The text surveys three alternative discrete state representations (referenced by three figures) and states that the chapter uses the first representation while others are reserved for later work. It also notes the abstract and flexible nature of MDP design, lists the necessary components to formulate an MDP for this electromagnetic design problem (system dynamics, agent training, reward design), and warns about problem complexity (countable state/action sets and unbounded reward space). Two additional figures illustrate negative reward scenarios and potential design errors from leaving the designated design space. This subsection introduces and formalizes value functions used in reinforcement learning, focusing on the action-value function Q(s,a) and the state-value function V(s). It defines Q(s,a) as the expected return G_t when taking action a in state s and presents the recursive return G_t = R_{t+1}+G_{t+1}. The text motivates using Q(s,a) for this work (because transitions can be achieved in multiple ways and Q facilitates action comparison), contrasts Monte Carlo methods (which use full-episode returns) with temporal-difference (TD) bootstrapping (which updates incrementally using estimated next-state values), and gives TD-style update formulas including the max-based target used in Q-learning. It also introduces discounting (γ) to downweight distant rewards, and notes that TD methods converge faster but trade off higher variance/possible bias compared to MC, while relating TD to both Monte Carlo and dynamic programming principles.

A LaTeX subsection titled “Bellman Equation” in Chp4_MDP that defines the Bellman optimality equation for action-value functions: Q(s,a) = r(s,a) + γ max_{a'} Q(s',a'). It explains key RL concepts related to this equation: the notion of a policy π(a|s) (including greedy policies), the distinction between on-policy and off-policy learning, and that Q-Learning is an off-policy algorithm which uses the Bellman optimality equation to learn the optimal action-value function Q* directly (avoiding separate policy evaluation and improvement). This subsection precedes the Q-Learning section.

This LaTeX section (Chp4_MDP::Q-Learning) explains and defines the Q‑learning component used in the chapter’s MDP framework. It: 

- Introduces the policy concept (policy evaluation vs policy improvement) and defines action‑value functions Qπ(s,a) and deterministic/greedy policies.  
- Describes Q‑tables (a tabular representation of Q(s,a)) and shows that the optimal policy is obtained by taking argmax_a Q(s,a). A sample Q‑table and illustrative figures are included.  
- Presents the Q‑learning update rule (TD style): Q(s_t,a_t) ← Q(s_t,a_t) + α[ R_{t+1} + γ max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a') − Q(s_t,a_t) ], and explains its components (learning rate α, discount γ, TD target, off‑policy max).  
- Defines ε‑greedy exploration and the exploration–exploitation tradeoff, including practical guidance on ε scheduling (start high, decay to a small value) and why pure greedy selection can be suboptimal.  
- Contrasts Q‑learning with Dynamic Programming and Monte Carlo methods: notes MC estimates from full episodes, their computational cost and need for simulation (e.g., EM simulator for field states), and highlights Q‑learning’s incremental, bootstrapped updates (TD) and its suitability when environment dynamics are unknown.  
- Mentions practical limitations: tabular methods fail in high‑dimensional or continuous state representations (necessitating function approximation), and treats ε schedule and related parameters as hyperparameters.  

Overall, the section provides the conceptual basis, update mathematics, and practical considerations for applying Q‑learning in the MDP problems studied in the thesis (including topology/EM optimization examples).

This LaTeX subsection defines and explains the policy function in the MDP/Q‑learning context. It distinguishes policy evaluation (estimating value functions under a fixed policy) from control/policy improvement (searching for a policy that maximizes return), defines a (stochastic) policy π(a|s) and the special case of a deterministic policy π(s)=a, and shows how the optimal Q(s,a) yields an optimal (argmax) policy. The text presents the Q‑learning TD update (with learning rate α, discount γ and an off‑policy max over next‑action Q) and describes ε‑greedy action selection (probability ε random exploration, 1−ε greedy exploitation), including practical notes on starting/decay/minimum ε as hyperparameters. It discusses the exploration–exploitation tradeoff, the need for sufficient coverage of state–action pairs, and the limitation of tabular methods for high‑dimensional or continuous state representations (motivating function approximators). The subsection includes illustrative figures/tables (deterministic policy diagram, example Q‑table, and search tree) and cites the origin of Q‑learning.

Defines the ε-greedy exploration strategy used by the Q-learning–based controller to balance exploration and exploitation. At each time step t the agent selects the greedy action argmax_a Q_t(s,a) with probability 1−ε and otherwise picks a uniformly random action with probability ε. The subsection explains the role of ε (ranging from 0 to 1), common scheduling practice (start with a high ε near 1 to encourage early exploration, then decay to a small floor such as 0.05), and treats the start value, decay rate, and stopping value as hyperparameters. It also notes the exploration–exploitation trade-off and that in MDPs an optimal deterministic policy exists.

A short LaTeX subsubsection that explains the exploration–exploitation trade-off in the MDP context. It also highlights practical limitations: tabular methods fail for high‑dimensional or continuous state representations (e.g., including magnetic field values), and therefore function approximators are required — a topic deferred to Chapter 5.

\subsection{Topology Optimization}

The most noticeable advantage of the Topology Optimization (TO) is its capability of free-shape optimization, which can outperform template-based design optimization routines in terms of the speed of the process if well-tuned. 
However, the majority of the TO techniques introduced in the literature result in solutions that are not easily manufacturable, i.e., the optimized design has checkerboard patterns, floating or stray pieces of material.
To overcome this difficulty, either different filtering or smoothing methods are employed \parencite{campelo2008} or smoothness of the solution is added as an objective of the optimization process itself \parencite{dupre2014ant}. A new TO method (sequence-based) is proposed in Chapter \ref{chapter:4_MDP} which ensures that the final optimized solution does not have any checkerboard patterns, perforations, or floating pieces of material. This method leverages a sequence-based environment to impose connectivity on cells containing the same material. This proposed methodology neither requires any filtering or smoothing technique nor any modification to the optimization objective function for obtaining manufacturable optimal solutions. 

Building on the proposed sequence-based TO methodology, in the next chapter (Chapter \ref{chapter:5_RL}), the concept of an intelligent agent is investigated in the field of TO by means of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms. The agent is trained in an interactive manner of learning such that the topology of the geometry is basically an iterative process involving continuous interaction between an RL agent and a FE-based environment. The process involves an incentive-based generation of a number of design structures as output that satisfies the design requirements and objectives determined by the designer at the highest level of the design process.

The intuition behind this sentence is that every model is wrong because it is a simplification of reality. However, simplifications of reality can be quite useful. They can help us explain, predict and understand the universe and all its various components. It means useful insights can be provided from models which are not a perfect representation of the phenomena they model. The practical question is how wrong do they have to be in order to be not useful. As such, the desirable features of a model can be summarized as follows \parencite{silva2018}:

\begin{itemize}
    \item A model should be consistent in its ability to explain past observations and predict future observations.
    \item Cost of usage: A model should be computationally cheaper than traditional methods available for analysis. 
    \item Level of accuracy in the prediction: A model that gives highly accurate results but takes a lot of computational time may not be useful. On the other hand, a model that is not as accurate but can produce estimates very quickly can be beneficial.

A GA can start with a random population, and this eliminates dependency on any initial user input. However, to accelerate convergence, sometimes an initial population may be specified if it is known beforehand that the optimal result may lie close to it. This is a choice which is very specific to the expectations and the aim of employing a GA to solve a particular optimization problem.

From a random initial population, the next step is to identify which individuals are best suited to reproduce and evolve the next generation. For this purpose, various genetic operators are applied to the current population. The aim of applying these operators is to efficiently and effectively scout the search space.
The genetic operators commonly used are described as follows:

\begin{itemize}
\item Reproduction
\\The individuals with the highest fitness values in the population are selected to produce offspring and create the next generation. The individuals selected for reproduction are known as parents while the new individuals generated using them are called children. A select few individuals with the best fitness values are retained as they are for the next generation, in addition to acting as parents. This process is known as elite selection.

\item Crossover
\\After reproduction, pairs of parent individuals are randomly selected to mate, and then the genetic information of the pair is swapped at a randomly determined crossover point along the length of each string (chromosome) to create a new child individual, which thus has a combination of genes of both parents \cite{GA2007}.
This process is called crossover and it allows exploitation of the search space to find better solutions.

\item Mutation
\\This involves introducing random changes to one or more genes in the chromosome of a parent individual so as to explore the whole search space and not let the algorithm get trapped in a local minimum. This helps maintain genetic diversity and randomly distribute the genetic information \cite{GA2007}.
\end{itemize}

The genetic operators discussed in the preceding section are applied iteratively, evolving a new generation of individuals every iteration. Theoretically, the GA may be able to find the global optimum value of an objective function only if it is run for a length of time that is long enough to evaluate the fitness of all possible individuals in the design domain. For the size of the optimization problem under consideration ($288$ variables, with each variable allowed to assume a value of either $0$ or $1$, i.e., $2^{288}$ possible individuals in the design domain), it would practically take an infinite length of time. Therefore, it is important to select the conditions that must be satisfied in order to terminate the GA. There are a few criteria which help in deciding when to stop this process. The convergence criteria depend on the optimization problem being solved and a couple of test runs may be required in order to select one.
\begin{itemize}

\item Generation Count
\\The GA is allowed to run for a fixed number of generations and is stopped after this required maximum generation count is achieved.

\item Elapsed time
\\This entails the GA being stopped after a certain period of time has passed, no matter the number of generations reached.

\item Stall Generation limit
\\If there has been no reasonable change or improvement in the fitness value for a fixed number of consecutive generations, the GA is stopped. 

\item Stall Time limit
\\The GA is stopped after a certain time during which there has been no significant change in the fitness value.

\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

This research aimed to explore the feasibility of modern statistical learning techniques for aiding the design optimization and analysis of electric devices and machines. A number of statistical learning methods, including supervised, bayesian and reinforcement learning have been used in the process. 

The first objective of the thesis was to use modern Deep Learning models to reduce the time spent in analyzing field and performance maps for low-frequency electromagnetic devices as compared to conventional high fidelity solvers based on first principles such as the Finite Element method. The high computation demands of high fidelity FE solutions can limit the effectiveness of these analyses and thus the ability to explore new design possibilities. As an example, for estimating the efficiency map of a single motor drive topology, many operating points need to be simulated using finite element analysis. Thus incorporating the whole efficiency map into the design optimization process is an overwhelmingly time-consuming task and may be impossible, depending on the availability of computational resources. For specific applications in the field of computational electromagnetics, the first section of this thesis (Chapter 2 \& 3) focuses on designing deep learning strategies for computationally inexpensive and accurate predictions of field distribution and performance maps of electric machines. It is demonstrated that DL algorithms can serve as an ideal venue for fast and precise solutions with sufficient training data. In the process, it was observed that this approach faced the issue of non-reliability and extended time spent in generating data. At times, creating massive datasets using Finite Elements simulations can be too expensive and can take weeks and at times months. For handling the enormous requirements of big data, an information transfer strategy between similar problems referred to as Transfer Learning is also implemented. This is verified with application to two test cases - $\eta$ map to $pf$ map prediction of same motor topology and $\eta$ map to $\eta$ map knowledge transfer for different motor topologies. Overall, a reduction of about 40-60\% in overall data requirement was experimentally observed for the two test cases. In scenarios where the NN is not sure about the prediction, a study involving uncertainty analysis in the predictions of DNN is also performed using Bayesian learning. 

The other objective of this thesis involved design optimization, where the excessive time spent in the optimization and manufacturability aspect of the optimized design is addressed. A new TO method (SeqTO) was introduced, which inherently generates manufacturable designs, free from checkerboard patterns, perforations or floating pieces of material and requires significantly less computational resources (around 80\% lower) as compared to using the same optimization algorithm with the ON/OFF discrete method. The SeqTO environment also serves as the platform for exploring tree search-based heuristic algorithms such as Monte Carlo Tree Search and TD-learning, which further reduces the computation burden by about 5-15 \%, compared to using a GA with SeqTO on the same design problem. Leveraging the sequential nature of the controller offered by the SeqTO environment and the pattern learning ability of a NN, a Reinforcement learning agent is also trained, which can generalize to different design parameters, even when such design parameters were unseen during the training phase. It is verified through numerical optimization that the trained agent reduces the number of finite element analysis-based electromagnetic analyses significantly (about 10 times) when deployed for many excitation patterns compared to conventional optimization methods such as the evolutionary algorithms.

Although all the proposed methodologies in this work are capable of providing ``instant" solutions for electromagnetic devices, they can be easily extended to other applications where computer simulations play a prominent role in imitating physical laws across various engineering domains.

Overall the main contributions of the thesis revolve around advancing the usage of high fidelity analysis and designing techniques at an early stage of an electric machine development cycle (V-cycle) as envisioned in Chapter \ref{chapter:1_Intro} (Introduction) of this thesis. It is also aimed to provide practical guidelines and recommendations for successfully deploying modern statistical methods in this field.
